Uniform Title: Subodhamañjarī Manuscript: BHU C4255 Notes:
Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: April 7, 2012. Country of Publication: India.
Oṃ, salutations to Gaṇapati.
Now, the Subodhamañjarī is being written.

Through the investigation of perfect awakening, I pay homage to Nanda, who has attained the arising of awakening through the intrinsic nature of meditative cultivation, and who is the very abiding state of the self. (1)
This entire universe consists of nothing more than this group of five, beginning with form;
it is perceived by the five sense organs, beginning with the eye. (2)
The eye resides in the mind of embodied beings in all states;
it becomes dissolved for him for whom everything is dissolved.
Another method for its application has been taught by the Guru;
out of fear of the loss of that tradition, it has been composed by me.

The conventional usage consisting of conceptual constructions such as birth and so forth resides in the mind; in reality, they do not exist at all. Having ascertained this, one should proceed toward their pacification.
At the time of the union of semen and blood, the mind does not exist anywhere;
it is neither in the embryo nor in the fetus, nor is it situated anywhere within the body.
In the body, from the end of dwelling in the womb through childhood and likewise through youth, up until its exhaustion, decay, and destruction—that [self] is not perceived at all. (7)
Flesh is distinct, form is distinct, and the location of the hair and so forth is distinct;
since everything is seen as distinct, where in the body does the mind abide? (8)
When this has been stated after such investigation, birth itself is taught in that very context;
yet that [birth] does not truly exist by way of reasoning, nor does it appear to anyone at all.
The name given by his father was false, since his conduct was not consistent with it;
for if he were truly virtuous, many virtues would have manifested.
Thus, having ascertained that the nature of the mind is flickering and overwhelmed by false conceptualizations and mental constructions, one should understand it as such.
This restraint, which was previously described by the ancients through the practice of yoga for the sake of detachment,
is now taught by us without effort.
If there were anything to be grasped, the mind would then be dissolved into that; but because there is nothing else to grasp, the mind becomes tranquil within its own self. (13)
Just as when a dense mass of sound gradually dissolves away,
the mind, by virtue of depending upon it, becomes tranquil once that [sound] has ceased.
Whatever is captivating that comes within the range of hearing,
one should contemplate it with one-pointed focus until it has dissolved and brought about cessation.
In the same way, one should contemplate the loveliness of forms and other objects;
afterwards, one should not remember them as they have dissolved, once they have been augmented by the nature of the Self.
Thus, O God, understand the object of perception through immersion as it has been described by me; this first [stage], arising from grasping, is now clearly seen.
One should awaken the senses, which are the instruments of perception, by laughing;
likewise, there would be the destruction of passion through the diminution of hatred. (18)
There would be the loss of the nature of all passion from every perspective; likewise, one would be as impassioned as a wise man, and Bhairava would be as wicked as anyone. (19)
The sense organ, ungraspable and empty, dissolves into its own self;
when the activity of the senses has dissolved, that which remains alone is the dawning of supreme prosperity.
Therefore, having taken hold of the mind within that which is empty and devoid of conceptual construction,
and with the activities of the senses rendered motionless, true realization arises.
For a yogin who is constantly yawning and afflicted by hunger, what is meditated upon within him? At the very end, there would be only [the exhaustion of] that.
For one whose mental fluctuations have not dissolved and who gradually resorts to sleep, a complete obstruction of the head arises due to the non-perception of objects. (23)
To whatever extent one restrains the efforts involved in the movement of the feet,
the Supreme Self shines forth for one whose mental activity is free from conceptual construction.
Even while seated upon a seat, having reflected with effort upon whatever state has arisen, one attains tranquility in the absence of the house (of the senses). // 25 //
"Through the vital air (vāyu), I perform the movements and other functions of the body;
yet the vital air does not reside in the mind, nor does the mind abide in the vital air. (26)

For one who reflects upon entities in this way, the mind is not established anywhere; its mental fluctuations are entirely false, and it remains in the absolute alone. Wherever there may be a desire for objects such as food and the like—
One should fill them according to one's capacity, so that one becomes full and without dependence. || 28 ||
If something desired has been spoken and is somehow forgotten, by reconnecting with it once more, one shall attain liberation (kaivalya) in an instant. (29)
When a visible object such as a post or a person is perceived from a distance, it is conceptualized;
however, for one whose mind is well-ascertained, cessation quickly arises. (30)
Since one perceives the seer through the intellect by means of visible objects,
O child, one attains liberation through that vision by which [the self] is bound.

Having grasped all objects of knowledge through effort, and not [grasping them] by way of their own inherent nature, one should therefore become composed of consciousness, [realizing] that "everything is known by consciousness. || 32 ||
Furthermore, one should cause the heart to expand by drinking from the foreign land;
likewise, when the downward breath (apāna) has dissolved, the activity [of the mind] becomes attenuated.
By resorting to the path of the Suṣumṇā and awakening through the way of serenity, one attains peaceful consciousness in an instant by abandoning the six drops (bindus). || 34 ||

Through the friction of the two drops (*bindu*) arising from the movement through the left and right [channels], the Great Power (*mahāśakti*) at the End of the Twelve is said by the perfected ones (*siddha*) to be the source of bliss. (35)
When the wind ascends upward, there is an end to agitation and tranquility arises;
likewise, upon the dissolution of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), there is the absorption of the mind.
Having opened the mouth and remained for a moment with a mind free from doubt, the cessation [of the breath] arises through the vital functions being paralyzed. (37)
One should direct the mind between the navel and the genitals at the conclusion of sexual union;
as it dissolves there, the bliss of passion becomes waveless for a moment. (38)
The mind, filled with an abundance of bliss from embracing a heart-friend who has come from afar, attains tranquility in an instant. (39)
When a sound is uttered from afar, its meaning is not apprehended because it is not clearly determined;
even for one who is attentive, the cognition of that [meaning] arises as a diminished understanding. (40)

Through the massaging of the feet and embracing, the obstruction of the mind shall come to an end; establish the perception of the six flavors and other objects upon the tip of the flickering mind. 41.
As the bliss of rasa wanes, absolute liberation (kaivalya) arises;
in the same way, one should contemplate the fragrances in jasmine and other such flowers.
By virtue of being dependent upon them, the mind dissolves when they have dissolved;
thus, at every moment, his mind dissolves into the Self. (43)
One who has attained awakening and possesses true being is designated as liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
This *Svabodhodayamañjarī* has been composed by Vāmanadatta, the son of Harṣadatta, that lion among the Mīmāṃsakas. 44.
